newsitem.title: UK: Options - Nearby, forward aluminium trade picks up.
newsitem.headline: Options - Nearby, forward aluminium trade picks up.

text.p: Aluminium options were in demand this week on the London Metal Exchange (LME), with falling underlying prices prompting covering of nearby put options.
There was also continued demand for at-the-money and upside calls in 1997, at times in good volume.
Copper option volatilities drifted despite falling values, as did options on most other base metal markets.
"We have seen nearby put buying on aluminium recently, concentrating on the $1,400 and $1,450 (a tonne) strikes," said one trader.
"Some of it was short-covering as a lot of market makers granted the puts as they didn't think the market would ever get down here," said another.

October aluminium volatility traded as high as 18.5 percent this week, although selling was starting to emerge in response to the higher levels. October was quoted at around 14 percent at the start of the week.
"You can get good prices for these options. If you get $60 or $70 for a $1,450 put, your exposure is all the way back below $1,400," one trader said.
Three month aluminium futures fell to $1,429 on Thursday, the lowest level for over two years.
Forward buying continued, with good-volume buying of at-the-money second-half 1997 aluminium calls.
"I don't know who is behind it - there may be a big play going on," said one trader.
Buying interest in 1997 has so far concentrated on upside calls, so some dealers played down the possibility that the buying was market makers covering their short exposure.
"If this was the case they would be buying back $1,700 or $1,750 calls," a trader said.
Second half aluminium options traded up to 19 percent volatility this week from around 18 percent a week ago. Several traders said these levels presented a good selling opportunity.
Some traders said recent rumours of large metal options players considering downsizing operations could explain this week's activity on the forward aluminium options market.
But others said participants could be getting volatility on board as a covering excercise.

Market makers noted bearish sentiment creeping into aluminium in recent weeks. They said the fact that average 1997 upside call buying had started at around $2,000 some time ago but was now at only $1,700 was a good reflection of this.
Copper volatilities drifted lower on nearby months despite the drop in underlying prices to two-month lows this week.
"Market makers have volatility down here. They are long of $1,750, $1,800 and $1,850s," said one trader.
"The market is much more comfortable on the downside than on the upside," said another.
Traders used lower prices to increase their cover of upside strikes, where the market is still thought to be short.
"People are looking to buy back $2,100 and $2,150 calls in 1996 and early 1997," said one dealer.
"They are keen to avoid a repeat of what happened late in August and in early September," he added.
Prices rallied $230 in the run-up to the September options declaration, largely on hedging against short option positions.
Most other base metal options volatilities eased this week.
"On nickel we saw a few more bullish plays this week, but it has subsided," said a trader.
October volatility fell to around 31 percent early Friday from 33 percent a week ago.
Lead volatilities dropped, with October at 18 percent on Friday from 23.50 percent a week ago.
Dealers noted granting of nearby strangles and options selling generally.
Tin volatilities edged back while zinc was generally steady.
